stem: A factory has two machines M1 and M2 that operate independently. The probability that M1 breaks down in a given week is 0.1 and the probability that M2 breaks down is 0.2. What is the probability that at least one machine breaks down in that week?

per_option_rationale.rationale: P(at least one) = 1 - P(neither breaks down) = 1 - (0.9)(0.8) = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28.
Simply adding P(M1) + P(M2) = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30 ignores the double-counted intersection.
Computing P(both break) = 0.1 * 0.2 = 0.02 answers the wrong event (both break, not at least one).
Using only P(M2) = 0.20 ignores M1 and misidentifies which machine's probability to report.

explanation: At-least-one problems are best solved via the complement: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). P(neither breaks) = P(M1 fine) * P(M2 fine) = 0.9 * 0.8 = 0.72. So P(at least one) = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28.

explanation_sections.punchline: Complement shortcut: 1 - P(none breaks) = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28 beats listing cases.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: two independent events; at-least-one query. Decisive move: use complement. State assumption: machines are independent. Compute P(M1 works) = 0.9, P(M2 works) = 0.8. P(neither) = 0.9 * 0.8 = 0.72. Answer = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28.
explanation_sections.lesson: For at-least-one with independent events, always use 1 - P(none) to avoid double-counting.
explanation_sections.timing: 60 seconds. Trap: adding 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30 double-counts the both-break case. Spot this and switch to complement.
